metadata.engine: PEER'S Docker Container Misconfiguration Scanner v2.0
metadata.author: Mohammed Peer Siddiqui

findings.title: Unpinned Base Image (:latest or untagged)

context.risk: Using latest or unpinned base image allows unexpected breaking changes or compromised layers.

findings.description: Base image references :latest or lacks specific version pinning, exposing the build to supply chain drift and breaking changes.
findings.remediation: Pin base image to explicit semantic version or cryptographic digest (e.g. 'python:3.11.8-slim-bookworm@sha256:...').

findings.title: Deprecated MAINTAINER Instruction

context.risk: MAINTAINER instruction is obsolete; use LABEL maintainer instead.

findings.description: The MAINTAINER directive is deprecated in modern OCI and Docker build specifications.
findings.remediation: Replace 'MAINTAINER' with standard OCI label 'LABEL maintainer="..."'.

findings.title: Hardcoded Secrets in Environment Variables

context.risk: Hardcoded credentials in image metadata can be extracted with 'docker history'.

findings.description: Sensitive credentials (passwords, API tokens, AWS keys) detected directly in ENV/ARG instructions, permanently baked into layer history.
findings.remediation: Remove secret values from Dockerfile. Ingest secrets dynamically at runtime via Docker Secrets, Kubernetes Secrets, or HashiCorp Vault.

findings.title: Privilege Escalation Tools (sudo) Installed
findings.raw_instruction: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y openssh-server sudo curl

context.command: apt-get update && apt-get install -y openssh-server sudo curl
context.risk: Installing sudo provides unnecessary privilege escalation vectors within the container.

findings.description: Package management commands install 'sudo', allowing potential privilege escalation pathways inside the container.
findings.remediation: Do not install sudo or su binaries in production containers. Design workloads to run under strict least-privilege principles.

findings.title: Dangerous Port Exposure (SSH Port 22)

context.risk: SSH server exposed inside container violates single-responsibility principle and invites brute-force attacks.

findings.description: Container exposes SSH port 22. Containers should follow single-responsibility microservice architecture; remote management via SSH breaks immutability.
findings.remediation: Remove 'EXPOSE 22' and uninstall OpenSSH server daemons. Use container orchestrator exec commands (e.g., 'docker exec' or 'kubectl exec') for debugging.

findings.title: Use of ADD Instead of COPY for Untrusted Remote Archives

context.risk: ADD directive with remote URL or auto-extract archive risks MITM injection or zip bombs.

findings.description: Instruction uses ADD with remote URLs or local archives. ADD features automatic tar extraction and remote downloads that can lead to MITM or zip bombs.
findings.remediation: Replace 'ADD' with 'COPY' for local files. For remote downloads, use 'curl' or 'wget' with checksum verification within a RUN directive.

findings.title: Container Running as Root User

context.risk: Explicit root user directive enables full container privileges.

findings.description: Container executes as root (UID 0), granting full host root equivalency in unconfined namespaces and increasing breakout risk.
findings.remediation: Declare a non-privileged user and group using 'USER nonroot:nonroot' or explicit numeric UID (e.g. 'USER 10001:10001').

findings.title: Missing Container HEALTHCHECK Directive

context.risk: No HEALTHCHECK instruction declared; container availability cannot be dynamically verified.

findings.description: Dockerfile does not define a HEALTHCHECK mechanism. Orchestrators cannot automatically detect crashed, deadlocked, or hung application services.
findings.remediation: Define a HEALTHCHECK instruction (e.g. 'HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s CMD curl -f http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1').
